What it is

The paper's story: where it is used, its core idea and the real system demo.
Real-world use

A camera and a patterned display that show hot air and gas

Imagine a camera that shows a gas leak the moment it starts: over a factory line, or on a robot that drives up to the display.

what the camera shows

It shows The camera's view turned into a map of the air: bright where the plume bends light, dark where the air is still.

How to read it Bright colours mark the moving plume above the pan; the still air stays dark.

the authors' demo · a robot finds the display

It shows The authors' own demo: a robot with a camera searches for the display, drives to it and stops where the Moiré forms.

How to read it Top left says what the robot does; the inset at the lower right is the robot camera's own view.

Factory · Production line · Sensing World ›
Motivation

Heat plumes and gas leaks are invisible

  1. 1heat plumes, and gas leaks are invisible to human eyes and commodity cameras
  2. 2temperature and gas sensors provide only point measurements, responding slowly
  3. 3optical Schlieren systems rely on expensive mirrors, lenses, and knife-edge filters
  4. 4BOS requires dense, high-contrast, visually intrusive backgrounds
what BOS compares

It shows BOS's random dots, before and with the flow: where the air bends light, the dots seem to shift a little.

How to read it Compare the two halves: the shift is tiny, so BOS needs sharp, high-contrast dots to find it.

State of the art

Schlieren outside the lab needed high-contrast, visible backgrounds

  1. 1Background-Oriented Schlieren (BOS) mitigates these hardware constraints by replacing optical assemblies with patterned backgrounds
  2. 2existing BOS approaches have to use high-end SLR cameras with high contrast black-and-white backgrounds
  3. 3these constraints hinder both optical Schlieren and BOS from being deployed in uncontrolled environments

It shows The paper's Table 1 sets optical Schlieren, BOS and MoiréLens side by side, and only MoiréLens is both cheap and hidden.

How to read it Each row is one way and each column one need; a tick is good, a cross is bad, and a diamond is in between.

Background

Four terms used throughout

Schlieren imaging01

Schlieren imaging is an optical technique that visualizes invisible phenomena by detecting minute air-density variations

Refractive-index disturbance02

Airflow disturbances between the background and camera create refractive-index variations that bend light rays

Moiré pattern03

small geometric displacements yield large, measurable phase shifts in the fringes

Colour filter array (CFA)04

a Bayer CFA (typically RGGB) where each pixel captures only one color component

a Schlieren view of the plume

It shows A classical Schlieren view of a plume: light and dark streaks where hot air bends the light passing through it.

How to read it The bright and dark streaks follow the rising, wavering plume; still air shows a plain grey.

two grids, one coarse pattern

It shows Two fine grids of almost the same spacing, laid over each other, make a much coarser pattern: the Moiré.

How to read it Where the lines fall in step it is light, out of step dark; a tiny shift of one grid moves the coarse bands far.

Core idea

The camera's own pixel grid magnifies the light's tiny bend

  1. 1we employ a periodic high-frequency grid as the background
  2. 2its interaction with the CFA of standard CMOS sensors inherently generates Moiré patterns in recorded images
  3. 3MoiréLens converts subtle refractive-index variations into measurable Moiré phase shifts
the display's grid over the camera's grid

It shows The display's fine grid laid over the camera's 2-pixel colour filter grid: together they make coarse Moiré cells.

How to read it When the plume shifts the display's grid by less than a pixel, the coarse cells move far more: the shift is magnified.

Core idea · what to observe

A plume shifts the Moiré far more than the grid

Variations in air density or temperature induce refractive-index disturbances, which distort the background pattern captured by cameras

  1. The plume bends the light between display and camera
  2. The display's grid moves less than a pixel
  3. The Moiré cells move far more
  4. The map lights up where the plume is
  5. Your turn Drag the plume nearer the camera or farther

It shows The Schlieren map the camera makes: it lights up where the plume bends the light, so the invisible plume can be seen.

How to read it The colour runs from −40 dB (dark) to −3 dB (bright), and the map fades as the plume moves away from the camera.

Challenge 1 · misalignment

Small camera rotations distort the Moiré pattern

even small camera pose deviations can introduce misalignment between camera and background, significantly altering the resulting Moiré patterns

each type of rotation produces a distinct Moiré pattern deformation

  1. Yaw: the cells stretch sideways
  2. Pitch: the cells shrink and shear
  3. Roll: the cells shrink to a fine, faint checker
  4. Uneven cells make an uneven, unreliable map
Cell-size spread, no AutoMoiré –
Cells found, no AutoMoiré –
the grid as the turned camera sees it

It shows When the camera turns, the grid it sees shrinks or tilts against its pixel grid, so the Moiré fringes grow, shrink or turn.

How to read it Left: the two grids; right: the camera's view, with the fringes' direction for an aligned camera dashed.

Moiré cells, no AutoMoiré

It shows The magenta and green Moiré cells the camera sees: a small turn makes them uneven, which spoils the Schlieren map.

How to read it Even cells mean an aligned camera; the arc shows the turn now, and the spread says how uneven the cells are.

Solution 1 · AutoMoiré

AutoMoiré: a pre-warped grid and a target cell count

AutoMoiré pre-warps the fringe background so that the camera perceives an undistorted Moiré gridA homography is the map between two flat views; the display's chessboard gives it. The grid is then drawn through its inverse, so the camera's turn cancels out.

  1. The turned camera sees the chessboard warped; its corners give H
  2. New: the grid is drawn through H⁻¹, and the cells are even again
  3. A Fibonacci search tunes fb until m cells fill the ROI
  4. The cells stay even while the camera turns 10°
  5. Your turn Turn the camera; set m
Turn axis

It shows First the chessboard the camera sees, then the Moiré cells with AutoMoiré: even again, filling the dotted m × m target. At step 3, the target scale of Fig. 6.

How to read it Magenta and green are the cells, the dotted grid is the target, the box is the ROI, and the arc shows the camera's turn.

the target-scale search

It shows How AutoMoiré picks the grid's frequency fb: three tries find the fb that gives the target number of cells.

How to read it The line gives m for each fb, the dashed line is the target, and each numbered dot is one try of about 1 s.

Challenge 2 · visible fringes

A grid strong enough for the camera distracts people

Directly overlaying strong, high-frequency patterns into everyday wallpapers would be visually distracting in daily spaces

MoiréLens must isolate the Moiré patterns from the wallpaper texture and color, to prevent interference during processing

  1. A strong grid on the display: the camera sees it well
  2. A person in the room sees it too
  3. Fainter, and the person stops seeing it
  4. And a wallpaper's own texture mixes with the grid
Grid seen by the viewer –
what a person sees

It shows A strong grid on the wallpaper, as a person's eye sees it: close up it stands out, so it distracts in a home.

How to read it The stripes are as dark as the contrast the eye keeps while the viewer walks from 63 to 150 cm and back.

what the camera sees

It shows The camera's view of the same wall: the Moiré cells it needs. The camera does not need the grid to be strong.

How to read it Magenta and green are the Moiré cells in the a* colour channel.

Solution 2 · invisible embedding

Invisible embedding and colour Moiré separation

We exploit the insight that Moiré-based Schlieren imaging is less sensitive to background contrastSo a faint grid is enough; far away the eye blurs it out, though a viewer at 63 cm still sees it. In the paper's simulated test, a camera views 4,269 wallpapers from 60, 100 and 140 cm. The Moiré it takes from the wallpaper has an SNR over 3 dB for 72.8, 69.9 and 64.2 % of them.

  1. New: the grid mixed into the wallpaper
  2. At 180 cm the viewer sees no grid
  3. The camera's picture mixes wallpaper and Moiré
  4. The a* channel keeps only the Moiré
  5. Your turn Switch a*; set β, distance
Map SNR, wallpaper on –
Grid seen by the viewer –
LPIPS at β = 0.8, paper –
what a person sees

It shows The wallpaper with the grid mixed in, as a person sees it: from 1.8 m on, the grid can no longer be seen.

How to read it The darker the stripes, the more of the grid a person still sees. A far viewer and a small depth β make them fainter.

what the camera sees

It shows The camera's picture: with the a* channel only the Moiré cells are left, so the wallpaper does not hide the plume.

How to read it Magenta and green are the Moiré; with a* off, the wallpaper's light and dark are mixed in.

Challenge 3 · one setting

Moiré sensitivity varies across each cell and each flow

The sensitivity of Moiré-based Schlieren visualization is inherently spatially nonuniform

the center, where color gradients are minimal, responds weakly to refractive-index changes

  1. Each cell: weak at its centre, strong at its edge
  2. A slow leak: the frame difference sees almost nothing
  3. A plume under large cells falls on weak spots
  4. No single setting suits every flow
Map SNR at this setting –
Plume on sensitive spots –

It shows A setting tried on the wrong flow: the plume's setting misses the slow leak, and large cells leave the candle plume on a weak spot.

How to read it The colour runs from −40 dB (dark) to −3 dB (bright), and the words name the flow, the time filter and m.

where the Moiré is sensitive

It shows How strongly each point answers a 1-pixel shift: weak at each cell's centre, so a small leak there is missed.

How to read it Bright: sensitive (cell edges); dark: weak (cell centres); the outline is the plume.

Solution 3 · adaptive Moiré-to-Schlieren

Adaptive cell size and time filter for each flow

larger m values are used for global plumes, whereas smaller m values are used for regional airflowsm is the number of Moiré cells across the region watched. Small cells spread strong edges over a large plume; one large cell puts its strong edge across a small leak.

  1. Butane leak: m = 1, background subtraction
  2. One large cell puts strong edges across the leak
  3. Candle plume: m = 6, frame difference
  4. Small cells cover the whole plume
  5. Your turn Pick a flow, m, a filter

What you saw The paper's numbers are its effective sensing ranges (§6.1). Ours runs each row with background subtraction, as the paper does for gas leaks (Fig. 9).When m = 6, sensitivity concentrates near cell edges, resulting in more fragmented patterns and a reduced effective range.

Ablation study

Question Which module does a gas leak's SNR need most?The test is the paper's butane leak, 40 cm from the camera. The grid is in a wallpaper and the camera is rolled 10°. Each try switches one module off.

You change
MoiréLens's modules: one off at a time
  1. 1Your turn PressAutoMoiré pre-warps the grid for the camera's pose. Without it, a 5° roll leaves a fine checker of small cells, and a 10° roll leaves an almost even grey (Fig. 5).
  2. 2Your turn PressThe a* channel keeps the Moiré's colour and drops the grey wallpaper. Without it, the wallpaper stays in the image and adds to the noise (Fig. 7d, 7e).
  3. 3Your turn PressA cell is weak at its centre. With six cells across, many weak centres fall on the thin leak. One large cell keeps it on a strong edge (Fig. 8).
  4. 4Your turn PressFrame difference shows what changed since the last frame. A slow leak barely changes, so almost nothing is left. Background subtraction keeps the whole leak (§4.3.2).
More controls
Temporal mode
SNR, this try –
SNR, all parts on –

What you saw SNR: the Schlieren map's signal over its noise, in dB. We call the leak seen over 3 dB, the paper's bound for a stable Moiré extraction (§4.2.2). The leak's strength and the noise are our model's, set to the paper's ranges (Fig. 3, Fig. 11).As shown in Fig. 5, each type of rotation produces a distinct Moiré pattern deformation a monochrome camera with a standard ISP pipeline can automatically separate Moiré patterns from the wallpaper through color differentiation larger Moiré cells (m ↓) are preferable for regional airflow visualization MoiréLens employs two complementary visualization strategies: background subtraction for quasi-static phenomena (e.g., continuous gas leaks) and inter-frame differencing for dynamic flows Despite the visual overlay, MoiréLens delivers Schlieren visualizations comparable to using a pure Moiré stimulus

Comparison with related work

Question How does MoiréLens compare with BOS, the paper's baseline?BOS (background-oriented Schlieren) films random dots and finds how far the plume moved them. MoiréLens reads the same tiny shift as a Moiré phase. Both run in our simulator, on the paper's candle test.

BOS (Raffel 2015). Its error falls as the background's contrast C and its fine detail B grow.This is the paper's Eq. 2, from Raffel 2015 [23]: the shift's error grows with the image noise and shrinks as C times B grows. B falls as the camera moves away (§3.2). BOS papers: Hargather and Settles 2011 [13]; Richard and Raffel 2001 [24].

You change
the camera's distance s and the contrast C
  1. 1Your turn Drag the candle along the camera's lines is how far the camera stands from the candle. Drag the candle toward the camera and s gets shorter. The background stays 40 cm behind the candle, as in the paper's test, so you see the camera move, not the candle: in as s gets shorter, back as it gets longer.
  2. 2Your turn Or dragThe same distance s as the drag, in steps of 5 cm.
  3. 3Your turn PressFig. 3(b)'s test: the candle at 20 cm, the background's contrast lowered.

Go Beyond the Paper · 1 of 3

Generalization study

Question How far can MoiréLens see?The paper tests the candle to 140 cm (Fig. 3a) and the phone to 215 cm (Fig. 11). Here the plume goes to 300 cm, with either camera. A farther plume bends the light by the same angle, but the background moves less in the image. The shift in pixels is fx·d/(s + d)·α (the paper's Eq. 1). It falls as s grows. A camera with more pixels per degree, like the Pixel 9 Pro, sees a larger shift.

You change
the plume's distance, s
  1. 1Your turn PressAt 140 cm the paper's candle map is faint (Fig. 3a). The dot on the chart is the plume now.
  2. 2Your turn DragPast the paper's last test the chart is shaded. The readout says how far the plume is still seen.
  3. 3Your turn PressThe paper's phone saw butane and compressed air at 215 cm (Fig. 11, row 4). Its 4K video is 3840 pixels across, against the OV9281's 1280.
  4. 4Your turn Dragd is the distance from the wall to the plume. The paper says the result changes little with d (§5.1).

Go Beyond the Paper · 2 of 3

Physical conditions

Question Which change of the room or the camera lowers the plume's SNR most?The test is the paper's candle at 20 cm (Fig. 3b), with m = 6 and frame difference. Each tab changes one condition.

You change
the contrast, the embedding, the frame rate, the noise
ContrastEmbeddingFrame rateNoise
  1. 1Your turn Lower the contrast to 0.4.C is how strong the grid's stripes are. Dim light or a printed poster lowers it (§6.1). MoiréLens reads a phase, which C does not change; BOS reads dots, which fade with C (the paper's Eq. 2).
MoiréLens at this C –
BOS at this C –

What you saw In our model the Moiré's SNR falls with C as its colour fades, but less than BOS's, which also loses its fine dots.whereas the Moiré-based approach remains effective even at C = 0.4, since phase modulation of the grid is preserved regardless of C

  1. 1Your turn Raise β from 0.8 to 1.β is how strongly the grid lightens and darkens the wallpaper. The paper's Eq. 13 multiplies the wallpaper's brightness by 1 + β × the grid. A larger β gives a stronger signal. It also shows more to a person nearby. The paper picks β = 0.8 (§6.3).
SNR with the wallpaper –
Fringe seen at 180 cm –
LPIPS at 180 cm –

What you saw The fringe seen is our model of the eye: 60 pixels per degree (§6.3) and a blur we assume. The LPIPS is the paper's (Table 3), measured at β = 0.8 only.

  1. 1Your turn Pick 30 fps.The OV9281 runs at 100 fps (§5.1). Frame difference compares two frames. At 30 fps they are 33 ms apart, so the flickering plume has changed more.
    Frame rate
SNR at this rate –
Paper's oil temperature error –

What you saw The candle's flicker rate, 12 Hz, is our assumption. The paper's temperature errors: 7.10 °C on unseen powers at 100 fps; 10.30 °C at 30 fps, models retrained (§6.2.3, Fig. 14b).MoiréLens remains robust under reduced temporal resolution

  1. 1Your turn Raise the noise to 8 %.The noise of each pixel's a* value, as a share of the Moiré's own swing. The paper does not give it; 2 % is our value, set so that the ranges match Fig. 3 and Fig. 11.
SNR at this noise –
Seen up to –

What you saw Twice the noise takes 6 dB off the SNR. To win back those 6 dB, the plume must come much closer to the camera. The signal grows only slowly as the plume comes closer (the paper's Eq. 1).

  1. Heating power (W)the learned regressor is not re-made: the paper's numbers (Fig. 14(a)) are shown Fig. 14
  2. Range hood onthe learned regressor is not re-made: the paper's numbers are shown §6.2.3
  3. Printed background (a poster on the wall), with or without wallpaperthe model draws the digital display only; the printed poster's lower contrast (ambient light, no backlight), no AutoMoiré recalibration and its slight non-planarity are shown by the paper's Fig. 12 on the Real-to-Simulation Gap page §5.1; §6.1; Fig. 12
  4. The wallpaper's texture frequency and brightnessthe 4,269 wallpapers are not modelled: the paper's share over 3 dB (Fig. 7(f)) is shown §4.2.2; Fig. 7(f)
  5. Liquid temperature (°C)the learned classifier and regressor are not re-made: the paper's numbers by temperature (Fig. 13(b), Fig. 15(b)) are shown §6.2.2; Fig. 13; Fig. 15
